title: When Is Additional Retrieval Worthwhile? A Cost-Aware Study of Evidence Gain and Answer Reliability in RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can benefit from more sophisticated retrieval, but extra retrieval may be unnecessary for many questions and gains in evidence retrieval may not translate into faithful or correct answers. We study a cost-aware, two-action retrieval policy that chooses between a dense-retrieval-plus-reranking baseline and a hybrid lexical--dense retriever. Rather than classifying baseline retrieval as simply successful or unsuccessful, we estimate the question-specific incremental evidence-retrieval benefit of hybrid retrieval using features available before the routing decision. A regularized linear model and decision threshold are selected using document-grouped cross-validation and frozen prior to held-out evaluation. On 60 previously unseen QASPER training-split articles (188 questions, 169 evidence-evaluable), the policy triggers hybrid retrieval on 46 questions (24.5\%) and obtains the same evidence Hit@10 as always-hybrid retrieval (78.70\%, versus 76.92\% for always-keep). Paired, paper-cluster bootstrap intervals do not establish a reliable utility advantage. We further compare generated answers from a 4-bit Qwen3-4B model under the three retrieval policies. Provisional answer-level assessments show no clear correctness or faithfulness improvement after partial review, despite the evidence-retrieval result. The generation assessments remain model-assisted and lack independent human validation. These results expose an important distinction between retrieving relevant evidence efficiently and improving the reliability of the generated answer. The work is presented as a reproducible empirical study, not a claim of statistically established answer-quality superiority.

title: When Normalization Hurts: Quantifying Morphological Asymmetry Effects in Arabic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are increasingly used for Arabic question answering, yet applying morphological normalization to only one side of the query–passage pair has received little systematic study. We examine this normalization asymmetry on Mr. TyDi Arabic (3115 development queries; 2,106,586 passages) with a 2×2 design that applies Farasa segmentation to queries, passages, both, or neither under BM25, alongside dense and hybrid baselines and a fixed Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct reader. Asymmetric normalization reduces nDCG@10 by 10–39%; segmenting only the query costs 3.9× more than segmenting only the passages, and this retrieval pattern replicates on the held-out test split. An analyzer ablation supports the interpretation that segmentation creates the penalty, whereas the directional imbalance arises from its interaction with the Lucene ArabicAnalyzer. In the more damaging direction, the recall deficit persists through k=100, and a score-level diagnostic attributes collapses mainly to displacement by detached affix tokens. Generation metrics also decline significantly; the decline is much smaller than that of retrieval against a passage-prefix reference but roughly two to three times larger when answers are scored against TyDi QA minimal answers. An English-trained dense encoder performs no better than our BM25 configuration, so the large mE5 gain should not be generalized. Within this setting, consistency between query and passage normalization matters more than the choice of symmetric scheme, as the two symmetric schemes do not differ significantly.

title: When Quantization Affects Confidence of Large Language Models?
abstract: Recent studies introduced effective compression techniques for Large Language Models (LLMs) via post-training quantization or low-bit weight representation. Although quantized weights offer storage efficiency and allow for faster inference, existing works have indicated that quantization might compromise performance and exacerbate biases in LLMs. This study investigates the confidence and calibration of quantized models, considering factors such as language model type and scale as contributors to quantization loss. Firstly, we reveal that quantization with GPTQ to 4-bit results in a decrease in confidence regarding true labels, with varying impacts observed among different language models. Secondly, we observe fluctuations in the impact on confidence across different scales. Finally, we propose an explanation for quantization loss based on confidence levels, indicating that quantization disproportionately affects samples where the full model exhibited low confidence levels in the first place.

title: When RAG hurts: Retrieval-augmented generation degrades performance in metallurgical root cause analysis
abstract: Metallurgical failure analysis requires deep domain expertise to identify root causes from complex material evidence. This study evaluates the capability of large language models (LLMs) to perform automated root cause analysis in metallurgical failure cases, with and without retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We constructed a dataset of 195 failure analysis cases across nine metallurgical failure categories, each containing expert-extracted input narratives and ground truth root cause descriptions. Four configurations were evaluated on Xiaomi MiMo-v2.5: without RAG (non-RAG), with default dense RAG, with a filtered dense RAG pipeline that removed duplicate references, and with a lexical BM25 retriever; two additional models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash) were evaluated without RAG and with filtered RAG. For MiMo-v2.5, the non-RAG configuration achieved 76.4% CORRECT verdicts, against 69.2% (default RAG), 64.1% (filtered RAG), and 70.3% (BM25 RAG). The degradation was model-dependent: it was statistically significant only for MiMo-v2.5 ( Δ = 12.3 pp, McNemar’s p = 0.003 ), whereas the differences for the two DeepSeek models were small and not significant. Separate expert evaluation (three independent evaluators) indicated moderate-to-substantial agreement of the automated evaluation for both non-RAG outputs (70.0% agreement, Gwet’s AC1 = 0.58) and RAG outputs (84.0% agreement, AC1 = 0.78). We present plausible post-hoc explanations for the observed degradation, including semantic-mechanistic retrieval mismatch and reference-induced reasoning shifts, and we estimate API inference costs of approximately US$0.0006 per case per configuration for the four MiMo configurations (inference cost only, excluding an operational system). These results suggest that retrieval does not universally improve domain-specific LLM reasoning, and that in metallurgical failure analysis the penalty of an ill-suited retrieval configuration can outweigh its benefits.

title: Why Neighborhoods Matter: Traversal Context and Provenance in Agentic GraphRAG
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation can improve factuality by grounding answers in external evidence, but Agentic GraphRAG complicates what it means for citations to be faithful. In these systems, an agent explores a knowledge graph before producing an answer and a small set of citations. We frame citation faithfulness as a trajectory-level problem: final citations should not only support the answer, but also account for the graph traversal, structure, and visited-but-uncited entities that may influence it. Through controlled ablation experiments, we compare the effects of isolating, removing, and masking cited and uncited graph entities. Our results show that cited evidence is often necessary, as removing it substantially changes answers and reduces accuracy. However, citations are not sufficient, because accurate answers can also depend on uncited traversal context and surrounding graph structure. These findings suggest that citation evaluation in Agentic GraphRAG should move beyond source support toward provenance over the broader retrieval trajectory.

title: Why RAGs Hallucinate: Penalty-Aware Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems with Knowledge-Gap Canaries
abstract: Volume-based accuracy rewards retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems for guessing: a system that answers everything outscores one that declines when its knowledge base cannot support an answer. Building on the confidence-target analysis of Kalai et al. (2025), we present a penalty-aware evaluation framework for deployed RAG products, combining (i) asymmetric scoring (correct +1, wrong -4, abstain 0), (ii) knowledge-gap canaries, questions whose answers are verifiably absent from the knowledge base, so that any answer constitutes ungrounded generation from parametric memory, and (iii) a failure-attribution pipeline that separates retrieval, generation, and abstention-policy failures. Applying the framework to three commercial RAG systems and a no-retrieval baseline on SimpleQA-Verified (1,000 questions x 3 repeats, graded blind by a cross-family three-judge panel with 98.9% unanimity), we find that accuracy when answering is closely clustered across systems (97.0-98.0%), while canary violation rates differ roughly sixfold (16.7% vs. 98.1%). The systems are separated less by what they answer correctly than by whether they answer at all when they should not, and penalty-aware scoring reorders the volume-based ranking accordingly; the reordering is stable across penalty settings from k=1 to k=9. All code, configurations, transcripts, and judge votes are released for independent audit.

title: Wireless Agentic AI with Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Semantic Perception
abstract: The rapid growth of multimodal agentic AI and LLMs enables richer perception and decision making, yet bandwidth-limited multi-agent links hinder timely exchange of task-critical semantics. Existing approaches based on static compression or heuristic selection do not adapt to the receiver's current query or to contention on a shared channel, which leads to redundant transmission or missing task-critical details. We propose Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Semantic Communication (RAMSemCom), a receiver-driven framework that iteratively retrieves only high-resolution image patches most relevant to the active task when the initial downsampled summary is insufficient. A centralized Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) scheduler at the roadside unit coordinates per-agent patch budgets and timing under shared bandwidth and round deadlines, using semantic relevance and channel state to orchestrate concurrent requests. Retrieved patches are overlaid via a spatial-awareness layout to preserve scene geometry without full-frame transfer. In a multi-vehicle urban driving case study, RAMSemCom achieves earlier task completion and better performance than strong non-learning and token-level baselines under identical bandwidth and latency budgets.

title: XÂY DỰNG HỆ THỐNG CHATBOT HỎI ĐÁP TRÊN TÀI LIỆU KỸ THUẬT SỬ DỤNG RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION
venue: Tạp chí Khoa học Trường Đại học Mở Hà Nội
abstract: Bài báo trình bày quá trình thiết kế và hiện thực một hệ thống chatbot hỏi đáp trên tài liệu kỹ thuật dựa trên kiến trúc Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) nhằm giảm thiểu hiện tượng ảo giác (hallucination) và tăng cường khả năng truy vết nguồn thông tin. Hệ thống được xây dựng theo kiến trúc hai pha tách biệt: pha ngoại tuyến bao gồm nạp dữ liệu, làm sạch, phân đoạn văn bản, sinh vector nhúng và lập chỉ mục; pha trực tuyến thực hiện truy xuất ngữ nghĩa, xếp hạng lại, xây dựng ngữ cảnh và sinh câu trả lời thông qua mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn. Nghiên cứu triển khai và so sánh hai chiến lược phân đoạn (theo ký tự và theo cấu trúc markdown), ba chế độ truy xuất (dense, keyword, hybrid), mô hình nhúng đa ngôn ngữ BAAI/bge-m3 và mô hình xếp hạng lại BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3, đồng thời hỗ trợ hai backend sinh văn bản (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct cục bộ qua Ollama và Gemini 1.5 Flash đám mây). Trên bộ kiểm thử gồm 25 câu hỏi có gán nhãn về tài liệu viễn thông 5G, cấu hình dense retrieval đạt Hit@1 = 84% và MRR = 0,913; khi bổ sung bước reranking, Hit@1 tăng lên 92% và MRR tăng lên 0,960 trong khi Hit@3 duy trì ở mức 100%. Kết quả chứng minh rằng kết hợp truy xuất ngữ nghĩa dày đặc với xếp hạng lại Cross-Encoder là hướng tiếp cận hiệu quả cho bài toán hỏi đáp theo miền; đồng thời cơ chế file-based cache và fallback backend giúp hệ thống có tính khả thi cao trên hạ tầng phần cứng phổ thông.

title: You Truly Understand What I Need: Intellectual and Friendly Dialogue Agents grounding Knowledge and Persona
abstract: To build a conversational agent that interacts fluently with humans, previous studies blend knowledge or personal profile into the pre-trained language model. However, the model that considers knowledge and persona at the same time is still limited, leading to hallucination and a passive way of using personas. We propose an effective dialogue agent that grounds external knowledge and persona simultaneously. The agent selects the proper knowledge and persona to use for generating the answers with our candidate scoring implemented with a poly-encoder. Then, our model generates the utterance with lesser hallucination and more engagingness utilizing retrieval augmented generation with knowledge-persona enhanced query. We conduct experiments on the persona-knowledge chat and achieve state-of-the-art performance in grounding and generation tasks on the automatic metrics. Moreover, we validate the answers from the models regarding hallucination and engagingness through human evaluation and qualitative results. We show our retriever's effectiveness in extracting relevant documents compared to the other previous retrievers, along with the comparison of multiple candidate scoring methods. Code is available at https://github.com/dlawjddn803/INFO

title: YpathRAG:A Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework and Benchmark for Pathology
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on general tasks yet still hallucinate in high-barrier domains such as pathology. Prior work often relies on domain fine-tuning, which neither expands the knowledge boundary nor enforces evidence-grounded constraints. We therefore build a pathology vector database covering 28 subfields and 1.53 million paragraphs, and present YpathRAG, a pathology-oriented RAG framework with dual-channel hybrid retrieval (BGE-M3 dense retrieval coupled with vocabulary-guided sparse retrieval) and an LLM-based supportive-evidence judgment module that closes the retrieval-judgment-generation loop. We also release two evaluation benchmarks, YpathR and YpathQA-M. On YpathR, YpathRAG attains Recall@5 of 98.64%, a gain of 23 percentage points over the baseline; on YpathQA-M, a set of the 300 most challenging questions, it increases the accuracies of both general and medical LLMs by 9.0% on average and up to 15.6%. These results demonstrate improved retrieval quality and factual reliability, providing a scalable construction paradigm and interpretable evaluation for pathology-oriented RAG.

title: ZenBrain v2: Preregistered Improvement Hypotheses. A same-day retrieval baseline on LoCoMo, three predictions closed before publication, and eight levers registered before they are built
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A preregistration that is written after a first measurement has to keep two things apart: what was measured before registration, and what is registered before measurement. This record does both for the retrieval stage of ZenBrain, an agent memory system, and marks throughout which numbers existed before the protocol was fixed and which do not yet exist. Measured (13 September 2026). All arms were re-run on one day, on one local embedding backbone (nomic-embed-text, 768 dimensions), on one benchmark (LoCoMo, 1,986 questions), at k = 5, with a verified reset and no paid model call. Three predictions about the system's own fifteen-flag configuration were written at 10:26:53 local time, before any arm had finished, and committed to version control at 10:40:05, before the cosine and ablation arms they are judged on had finished (10:45:34 to 11:06:24). One fell: removing every flag raised precision at 5 by 0.725 percentage points, short of the registered threshold of 0.75. Two held: one mechanism, the priority map, accounts for 93 % of that gap, and with the two hash-seeded mechanisms removed the arm's hit lists are identical to plain cosine search. The baseline for everything that follows is therefore cosine search, precision at 5 = 0.0885 — third of the four systems compared on that day (letta 0.0917; mem0 2.0.20 with hybrid retrieval 0.1046 to 0.1080 across three seeds; a-mem 0.0442). Registered (not measured). Eight levers — a content-derived importance signal in place of the hash-seeded factor, a repaired access counter, maximal marginal relevance, hybrid BM25 + dense retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion, fact-augmented key expansion, time-aware query expansion, a cross-encoder reranker, and query decomposition — each with target pool, expected delta and its source, test and decision rule; and one deferred lever (graph memory). The decision rule is common to all: comparison only against the cosine baseline re-measured on the same day, a noise floor of 0.25 percentage points, retention at three times the floor (a permutation p-value on the per-question differences is reported but decides nothing), and a second benchmark (LongMemEval) before any statement outside this registry. Stopping rules say when a lever is reported as inert or not evaluable rather than as a null result. Results for the first two levers are reported in Amendment 4 and in the data record it names; levers that fail remain in the registry with their numbers, as registered. Version 2 (13 Se

title: Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation via 3D Gaussian Splatting-Enhanced Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Existing end-to-end approaches of robotic manipulation often lack generalization to unseen objects or tasks due to limited data and poor interpretability. While recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate strong commonsense reasoning, they struggle with geometric and spatial understanding required for pose prediction. In this paper, we propose RobMRAG, a 3D Gaussian Splatting-Enhanced Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MRAG) framework for zero-shot robotic manipulation. Specifically, we construct a multi-source manipulation knowledge base containing object contact frames, task completion frames, and pose parameters. During inference, a Hierarchical Multimodal Retrieval module first employs a three-priority hybrid retrieval strategy to find task-relevant object prototypes, then selects the geometrically closest reference example based on pixel-level similarity and Instance Matching Distance (IMD). We further introduce a 3D-Aware Pose Refinement module based on 3D Gaussian Splatting into the MRAG framework, which aligns the pose of the reference object to the target object in 3D space. The aligned results are reprojected onto the image plane and used as input to the MLLM to enhance the generation of the final pose parameters. Extensive experiments show that on a test set containing 30 categories of household objects, our method improves the success rate by 7.76% compared to the best-performing zero-shot baseline under the same setting, and by 6.54% compared to the state-of-the-art supervised baseline. Our results validate that RobMRAG effectively bridges the gap between high-level semantic reasoning and low-level geometric execution, enabling robotic systems that generalize to unseen objects while remaining inherently interpretable.

title: ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.
